From: Ron Smith

Thanks for answering my query on
LOADing PCG's DTP to SAM but
your suggestion on altering the
LOADing instructions for the
code i.e. LOAD "WM" CODE in the
PCG's BASIC didn't do the trick.

As you know I am trying to copy
the program from PLUS D disc to
tape which you have to do before
LOADing into SAM via LERM's
SAMSPEC. LERM says it can be
done.They sent LOADing instruct-
ions but all I get after BASIC
has LOADed to tape is WORD at
the top of screen and nothing
after that,a complete freeze up.

I know it can be done but how?

The microdrive disc instructions
in the BASIC I think contain the
fault because if you add a line
at the start like 5 GOTO 100 and
then SAVE BASIC with...
SAVE"WORD"LINE 5 it LOADs code
but crashes at the end and
reverts back to the SAM LOGO.

I have enclosed the SPECTRUM
BASIC listings for the DTP.

OUTLET 47 is another great disc.
How you keep doing it I don't
know. Keep up the good work.
Cheers.

          Kind Regards,

            Ron Smith

Brian Cavers to Ron Smith

Remove the POKE @6,1 from line
100! Alter lines 20 to 50 to...

20 REM LOAD : RANDOMIZE USR x

30 REM SAVE : RANDOMIZE USR x

40 REM ERASE: RANDOMIZE USR x

50 REM CAT  : RANDOMIZE USR x

Once transferred, study your
SAMSPEC manual if you have no
further specific info from LERM
on the WORDMASTER conversion. It
is not easy but there is no
point in my duplicating the LERM
manual here but roughly you need
to do the following...

NONE of the LOADs and SAVEs etc.
will work from Spectrum BASIC to
the SAM drive. The LOADs and
SAVEs in the BASIC need to be
changed to POKE the CODE values
(s and l)into memory.I think you
also POKE a flag byte to tell
SAM BASIC whether you want to
LOAD or SAVE etc. (e.g.,1=LOAD,
2=SAVE, 3=ERASE, 4=CAT).

You then add a NEW which returns
you to SAM BASIC which should
then PEEK the addresses you
POKEd in Spectrum BASIC (PLUS AN
OFFSET OF 65536 I think) and
then SAM BASIC accesses the disc
and returns you to Spectrum
BASIC. Write again if you still
can't get it to work.
                        - Brian

From: John Powell, SALFORD.

Dear Ron & Brian,

OUTLET is truly great value for
money.

The game 'SHANGHAI' in Issue 46
was amazing - utterly addictive.
Whilst the general quality of
OUTLET has always been high, in
my opinion, this program is
really in a class of its own.

Whilst I'm writing this on
'OUTWRITE' can I mention a bug
in an otherwise excellent piece
of software. You will have
noticed that I like to indent my
paragraphs and have right just-
ification. This is not achieved

when wordwrap occurs on an
indented line. A gap is left at
the end of the line which I then
have to space out manually, as I
have done in this letter.

Keep up the good work!

        Yours sincerely,

           John Powell


Thanks, John. The indent bug is
new to me and I've made a note
to inform Bob Wilkinson next
time I write.

From: John Hutchings, NUNEATON

Just a few lines to congratulate
you and Mr. Wilkinson for the
production of OUTWRITE. I have
found it perfect for all my
needs from letters, minutes,
reports and I have even already
used it to produce a 50-page
journal of our recent twinning
visit to Roanne, Nuneaton's twin
town in France.

I just can't understand the
criticisms I've read in OUTLET.
It does all I need and more. I
am a PC user at work and
sometimes have the occasion to
use 'WORDSTAR' which as far as I
can see is no better and
probably costs 20 times as much.

The colour change facilities,
the print options and the
character fonts are a real bonus
but I think the biggest plus I
have found is its ability to
accept TASWORD files including
those generated by LERM.

My only suggestion for improve-
ments would be that:-

The name of the LOADed file be
displayed somewhere at the top
of the page - I overwrote the
wrong file on one occasion.

Obviously I haven't tried all
the facilities yet but so far I
am very pleased. Many thanks.

         John Hutchings

Brian Cavers to John Hutchings

Thanks John. I note what you say
about the filename being shown
at the top of the page. This is
one of those personal preference
customisation things though. It
is almost possible to do a short
mod from BASIC but not quite I
don't think. Anyway, it will be
considered.

                       - Brian

From Mr. B.H. Roper, SURREY

Dear Sirs,

Thank you for your prompt
attention to my request for
"OUTWRITE". The program is very
easy to understand and I have
also been able to amend the
printer control codes to suit my
own printer (Star SG10).

However, there is one main
problem which should be obvious
when reading this letter! The
text does not get printed in the
centre of the page. This is the
case despite amending the
printer control codes referring
to the left hand margin. Can you
help?

There is also a minor point that
I would like to mention and that
is the apparent inability to go
back to the first menu once the
text editor has been accessed.
Is this deliberate or an
ommission?

Once again I would like to state
how good the program is (once my
main point above is cleared up).

Whilst writing, I would also
like to thank you for "OUTLET".
I do enjoy receiving the disc
every month. There is only one
criticism,I cannot read "OUTLET"
on the way to work on the train!

I await your response in due
course.
              -  B. H. Roper

Brian Cavers to Mr. B.H. Roper

Let's go over exactly what is
happening...

Without changing anything, using
OUTWRITE as received, you do not
get ANY margin (even though the
program prints 8 spaces at the
start of each line by default).
Please confirm this is the case.

You are pressing EDIT then Z to
get the printer sub-menu and
then you are changing the left
margin setting and still getting
no margin. Again, please confirm
and state what margin you are
entering at this input.

I don't see how it can fail.

The only other thing I can think
of is that you are setting one
of the user-defined codes or
altering one of the existing
codes to send the codes for the
left-hand margin from within a
document. Please confirm if this
is the case. If so, please give
details of your printer's code
(if Epson-compatible then it's
27,108,n) and exactly what you
are POKEing.

To return to the first menu just
press EDIT then Q to quit the
text editor (see help page and
the manual).

                       - Brian

From Alan D. Cox, DYFED

Dear Ron and Brian

(i) I was surprised Ian Kennedy
was having trouble loading The
Last Word into SAM using
Specmaker. I have checked that
mine works OK (except that I
have problems with printer
initialisation because the HR5
does not have a command to do
it!). I do not know what to
suggest - the only comment I can
offer is that I used version 2.8
of Specmaker and I suppose it is
just possible that earlier
versions do not work. If Ian
wants, I would be happy to give
him my version of TLW - pity he
is so far away.

(ii) I note D.J.Manly's (or
Manning - you have got both)
comments on QUILL on a PC. He
does not say what particular PC
he bought and the older ones are
indeed slow. However, before I
retired I and my group (of about
20) used QUILL and the rest of
the PSION package on Apricot XEN
80286s without any complaints -
indeed, it knocked the spots off
many other WP programs,
including Wordstar.

(iii)I was very pleased to see
the letter from Simon Greenfield
complaining about SCPDSA and the
high-handed approach of Mr
Stevens. As you know, I am the
other complaint that he has
received.

I am surprised he has had so few
- I thought SAM/Spectrum users
were more discerning!. I do not
dissent from the general tenor
of Brian's comments insofar as
he says that Stevens is entitled
to lay down his own rules about
what he sells (or that his
authors are, since as I under-
stand it, he is only selling
others people's work). What I
object to is that he has hi-
jacked the phrase'Public Domain'
software and given it his own
erroneous interpretation.

Brian expresses doubts about the
average Spectrum user's under-
standing of 'Public Domain', but
in fact it is a not uncommon
phrase, not exclusive to 16-bit
or any other computers.

My Chambers dictionary says
(selecting the relevant defini-
tion):"the status of a published
work or invention upon which the
copyright or patent has expired
or which has not been patented
or subject to copyright. It may
therefore be freely used by the
public".

If we are looking for a computer
related definition, what better
than the words of Rod Smith, who
runs a PD set-up for PCs, in his
article in the first edition of
Computer Shopper: "With public
domain software, the author has
placed the program or its
copyright "in the public
domain". In essence, she/he has
said that anyone who would like


a copy of this program is
welcome to it, and to use it in
any way they see fit. Most
authors, however, exclude
selling the program or including
it as part of some other product
that is sold.....".

Normal practice is that one pays
the costs of the provider of the
PD software in furnishing the
program - disk, postage,
overheads - plus reasonable
profit margin- but one does not
pay for the program itself.

In this sense, therefore,
nothing that Stevens is selling
is anything like PD, since he
(or his authors) are charging
for the programs themselves - as

you are even for your FREEWARE
(and I do not object to this,
since you do not call it PD,
although you do imply in your
response to Simon that FREEWARE
is PD software - it clearly is
not unless you are prepared to
let anyone have a copy purely
for your costs).

There is a second issue, of
course, and that is the quality
of the software that Stevens is
selling. Although I have my own
opinion, I would only ask any
doubters to compare the SCPDSA
demo disk (which I assume is
meant to be typical of what he
is selling) and, say, WORM DEMO
in last month's OUTLET.

I will only comment briefly on
the ludicrous defence by Stevens
of the use of protection on his
demo disk - all I would say is
that I sent off my money for a
demonstration of what he was
selling, not a childish example
of how cleverly he has protected
his disk.

It is worth commenting that in
what I would call 'real'
personal computing i.e., PCs and
compatibles, the trend is very
much against copy protection.

(iv) Finally (I promise!) - not
SAM or Spectrum business, but I
am sure that some of your
readers have wider interests -
could you ask whether anyone


knows about machine code
programming for the 6301 CPU in
the EPSON HX20. It is a
fascinating little portable,
with built-in display, printer
and cassette recorder, but is a
bit slow, so machine code might
be worthwhile.

                  Alan D. Cox

Brian Cavers to Alan Cox

Thanks, Alan.

I don't deny that the expression
"public domain" is not exclusive
to the computer scene but I do
not think Mr. or Ms. Average
would have been familiar with
the phrase (or more especially,
"PD") back in 1987/88 when we
started FREEWARE.You may be more
literate than average withut you
realizing it. Anyway, I won't
pursue this point!

I must confirm our claim that
OUTLET software marked"FREEWARE"
really is public domain since it
is declared to be so and users
are genuinely able to copy it.

If we, or anyone else, sell a
piece of public domain software
"outside of the rules", such an
act does not affect the status
of the product. If I order a
piece of PC software that the
author has declared to be PD
then I could sell if for a
thousand pounds and it would not
change the fact that it is PD.

In any case, it is arguable that
we are charging a commercial
price for our PD. There may be
one or two items out of 20 or 30
in an OUTLET issue that are PD
so it could be said they are
"given away free with the
magazine" or that each PD item
only cost around 20p! Again, I
will not pursue the point!

I might ask in response to your
proviso:"unless you are prepared
to let anyone have a copy purely
for your costs", how much do you
think it would cost to produce
a disc magazine like OUTLET? It
is difficult to exclude tax and
advertising and labour costs as
well as the overheads associated
with running an office.

Finally, I think I speak for all
SAM and Spectrum users in taking
exception to your use of the
term "real" personal computing
as being exclusive to PC's as if
we were all playing in toytown!
I suspect you didn't mean it
quite like it sounded! Oh so,you
did, huh? Men have been hung up
by their function keys for less.
                        - Brian

          Chris Ingram,
     Box 5461, LIMBE, Malawi

To aid your market research I
would like to mention the
following programs as being of
special interest:

Leif Mortensen's 'CLIP ART' -
very useful in 'TYPELINER','PRO
CROSSWORDS' - for relaxing over

Remstored(6) for convenient

(33&44) is as useful as you said

Thank you for publishing my

On checking the disc with a

Do you think there is a fault

the 3.5" disc drive? The fault

Sorry to burden you once again

anyone else to turn to. I've

One final comment: the marketing
of double disc drives to fit the
Disciple and +D seems to have
ceased,judging by all the people
who need help converting their
interfaces to accept a second
drive. We tried to get double


drives last year for our school
computers; Datel told us they
were not available. I bought my
double drive from MGT not long
before they ceased operations
and have been very pleased with
it. I wouldn't like to have to
go back to using a single drive.
Making back-ups is so much
easier and I tend to keep odd-
numbered discs for drive 1 and
even for drive 2.

Are there any suppliers provid-
ing two drives in one case for
the Disciple/+D?

        Yours sincerely,

          Chris Ingram

From Brian Gaff to Chris Ingram

The disc corruption has happened
to me using a +D, and I suspect
that it is caused by a corrupted
BAM. (Bit Allocation Map).
Whether this occurs while the
Disciple is constructing it in
RAM or in one or more of the
directory entries on disc, I am
not sure. However, it means - as
you have seen - that sectors get
written to the wrong places.

The weird collection of errors
produced while trying to load
such files eludes me but I guess
the system gets conflicting info
when it tries to load them.Until
your letter, I had thought this
problem was peculiar to the +D,
caused by edge connector wobble.

I spoke to Nev Young about this
some time ago; the answer I got
was there is a bug in the +D ROM
when handling OPENTYPE files.

Apparently under some conditions
the ROM does not wait for the
motor to run up to speed before
writing to a sector. This causes
some corruption somewhere on the
disc. However, I do not think
this is the whole story, as this
should only give some sector
errors and an odd corrupted
file!

All I do is keep backups of
important files. If anyone can
shed any light on this, I think
there are at least two of us
dying to know the answer.

Double disc drives are less
common these days as most
computers already have one drive
inside. We will investigate this
situation though! You might try
looking at some magazines for
the BBC micro though!

                   - Brian Gaff

From: Stephen Wilson

Do you still suffer from your
disk-drives just spinning there?
I know the solution is to hold
in the reset button a little bit
longer when re-setting but what
happens if you forget and the
drive does it again - you can't
take out the disk or reset the
computer without corrupting the
disk - solution?? YES! - enter
OUT 224,220 and a second later
the disk drive will stop
spinning, enabling you to take
out the disk and reset properly.

What it does is tell the disk-
drive controller to stop its
current command, which would
have been to start up the motor.

I think it is a bug in the BOOT
command on ROM, - maybe a timing
error or something, I'm not
sure, but anyway, it seems to
startup the disk drive motor and
then proceed to move the head to
track 4, sector 1, (where DOS
USUALLY lies).  Try this. Put
DOS on a disk then completely
corrupt the first directory
entry - the disk STILL boots -
it ignores the file in the
directory but somehow the ROM
doesn't load in DOS, so it must
be a bug...)
                 Bye!
           Stephen Wilson


I've pencilled "OUT 224,220" on
top of my SAM...       - Brian

From: Derek Burn, BUCKS

Thank you for your comments on
my previous letter in OUTLET 47.
On reading them, I think that I
may not have expressed myself
very well, and I would like to
clarify my intentions.

Firstly, it was not my intention
to criticise OUTWRITE!. Far from
it. Neither do I believe that
there has ever been excessive
'hype' about its abilities. With
the issue of the enhanced
version 1.2, it is now a most
excellent word processor and I'm
sure that you are right to say
it will satisfy the needs of the
majority of Coupe users. I for
one am very happy to use it!

I had intended to address my
comments to a wider question
than software. What I had in
mind was the very general
question- whither the Coupe?

Let me explain.

When the Coupe was first issued
it had, apart from FLASH, no
software support. Given its
origins it clearly made
commercial sense to tap into the
existing vast library of
Spectrum software and so
considerable time and effort was
expended on the development of
programs which set out to make
the Coupe believe it was a 48K
Spectrum.

These efforts were generally
successful and most of the Spec-
trum's software can now be run
on a Coupe but it's still Spec-
trum software. That phase of the
Coupe's development is surely
essentially over -so what next?

I believe very strongly that the
Coupe is an excellent machine
which deserves recognition by a
wider public which I call, for
want of a better expression, the
'professional user'.

Consider for example the small
business man who may realise the
value a computer could be to him
but is reluctant to contemplate
the outlay that a PC, or other
16 bit machine, would involve.

The Coupe is perfectly capable
of fulfilling such a role, but
will only do so if an adequate
library of high-quality software
is available.

Hence my remarks about word
processing, which could be
expanded to embrace for example
desk top publishing, spread-
sheets, accounting programs and
so on. Happily there is evidence
this is beginning to happen; the
Coupe now has its own word
processors, databases and a
spread sheet, but I still do not
believe a 'professional user'
will feel adequately catered for
by what is so far available.
This is basically the reasoning
behind my use of the word
'worthy'.

Like yourselves, I too do not
believe the world owes us
anything, but I do firmly
believe that the 'Coupe' would
be more assured of the future
that it deserves with such
software.
           Derek Burn

Yes, well-answered Derek. I had
thought at the time of your
previous letter that it was a
case of missing the meaning.

Yes, whither the Coupe? The ST
took quite a while to build up a
degree of software. Good product
does take time to develop.I wish
I had time to devote myself to
one big project for six months
or so!
                        - Brian

From Jon Freedman, LONDON

OUTWRITE is quite an excellent
piece of software but a feature
that I do miss from Tasword 128
is the ability to type 128
columns of condensed text. Could
this be implemented?
                 - Jon Freedman

It is not practical to rewrite
OUTWRITE for 128 columns but if
you POKE 72000,128 and adjust
the left margin then you can get
it to print 128 characters. You
will need to switch off word
wrap and justification and split
words over the right margin. See
that odd-numbered lines have a
space at the end or the start of
the next! Clumsy but it works!
                        - Brian

From: Dave Marriott, NOTTINGHAM

Dear Ron & Brian;

Just a few words on 'Outwrite!'
I was hesitant about getting a
new word processor.I use Tasword
at home and 'Wordstart'at work
and sometimes get confused with
just the two of them! Also, I'd
just customised Tasword for
MasterDos.

However, I'm certainly glad I
got 'Outwrite!'

It seems author Bob Wilkinson
has started off by examining
Tasword to decide what was good,
what was bad, and what was
missing, then proceeded from
there.

The simplicity of the file
layout, the way in which help
pages and menus are called up
and the ease of customisation
will certainly make ex-Tasword
Users feel at home and you can
exit to BASIC to meddle about
then just type RUN to find your
text file mercifully intact.

'Outwrite' picks up where
Tasword left off. Gone is the
stubborn refusal to insert more
than one space in a line - you
can now shunt lines left or
right at will. Common options
like SAVE, LOAD and PRINT are
quicker to access and the key-
scan improved immeasurably. To
anyone trying to out-type it -
don't - you'll melt your
keyboard first!

I wasn't wild on the default
colours of white on black or the
PCW-type font, but then again we
are spoilt for choice as regards
alternatives - I found black on
green easiest on the eye and the
"No.6" font the most legible (in
fact,it's the most legible thing
I've read in SAM 64-column mode.

I've found one problem; for
"Form Feed" (Printer Options
submenu) it seems to send Hex 00
1B 0C 0D (NULL,ESC, FF, CR). My
printer, an Epson LQ400, takes
umbrage at the extra ESC and
doesn't do the Form Feed. Any
ideas for a Poke to fix it? If
you can't,the customisablilty of
the program means there's plenty
of other places to put a Form
Feed option.

Talking of printing, I do like
the way you can print a Pound
sign AND a Hash without the
usual hacking of code, prodding
of Dip switches and gnashing of
teeth in between!

With Tasman obviously not
concerned about any further
investment in a Sam version of
Tasword and Enigma still to
market their proposed program,
'Outwrite' could well become the
standard word processor for Sam.
It certainly deserves to be!

        Yours faithfully,

          Dave Marriott

Brian Cavers to Dave Marriott


The ESC code before the formfeed
is my own stupid fault and,as it
doesn't seem to affect my print-
er, it remained undetected. To
remove it, just LIST 817, EDIT
and DELETE it then use the SAVE
option from the menu. Leave the
CHR$ 0 which is harmless and is
used to get round the notorious
comms interface bug that ignores
the first code after switch-on.
I assume the bug is in the comms
interface - perhaps it's in the
SAM ROM. Does anyone know if the
same happens on the other avail-
able printer interfaces?

                        - Brian

From Norman Haigh, W. YORKS.



Dear Sir,

There is a problem with printing

### Brian Cavers отвечает Norman Haigh

Нет, шрифты в OUTWRITE меняют только отображение на экране, но не печать. Они предназначены исключительно для того, чтобы вы могли выбрать наиболее чёткий для ваших глаз вид на экране.

Если вы не хотите менять DIP-переключатель на принтере ради символа «#», можете попробовать следующее...

В TEXTMODE добавьте:

```text
;CHR$ 27;"R";CHR$ 0
```

после `CHR$ 08` в строке 1410, затем введите `RS`, чтобы сохранить изменения.

В TABLOID добавьте то же самое в конец строки 5150 и введите `RS`.

Пользователи Spectrum, желающие сделать то же самое, могут добавить этот код после «@» в одной из строк с 1400 по 1450 (в зависимости от синтаксиса вашей системы) в CONTENTS.

— Brian.
